title: Gramsci: Hegemony and the War of Position

cards.b: If capitalism is unjust, why do workers not simply revolt? Antonio Gramsci's answer: because rule rests on consent as well as force. His concept of hegemony is now used by historians, political scientists and activists far beyond Marxism.

Born in Sardinia (1891), small and sickly, Gramsci studied in Turin, edited L'Ordine Nuovo (1919-20), and backed the factory councils movement. He co-founded the Italian Communist Party (1921) and led it from 1924. Mussolini's regime arrested him in November 1926; the prosecutor said, "we must stop this brain from functioning for twenty years". He wrote 33 notebooks in prison (1929-35) and died in 1937, a few days after release from prison, aged 46.

In the Prison Notebooks (published 1948-51), hegemony is leadership by consent: a class rules when its worldview becomes common sense through schools, churches, press, family and culture, together forming civil society. Coercion (the state in the narrow sense) stays in reserve. "State = political society + civil society, hegemony protected by the armour of coercion."

cards.h: War of manoeuvre and war of position
cards.b: In Russia, the state was everything and civil society "primordial and gelatinous", so a frontal assault (war of manoeuvre) could win. In the West, civil society is a system of trenches and fortresses, so the left needs a long war of position: building alternative institutions, culture and alliances, before seizing power. This is read as a justification for democratic, gradual strategy.

cards.h: Organic intellectuals and the historic bloc
cards.b: Every class creates its organic intellectuals who give it awareness: factory technicians, journalists, union leaders. Traditional intellectuals (priests, professors) claim independence but serve the old order. A historic bloc unites classes around a common project; Gramsci worried about the "Southern Question": northern workers must ally with southern peasants. "Pessimism of the intellect, optimism of the will" is his slogan, borrowed from Romain Rolland.

Gramsci inspired Togliatti's Italian road to socialism and Eurocommunism, the New Left, Stuart Hall's cultural studies, Laclau and Mouffe, and Latin American politics (Evo Morales's MAS in Bolivia). Edward Said used hegemony to describe Orientalism. Political parties of the right also borrowed it: the "culture war" strategy of intellectuals in the 1970s and the New Right drew on Gramscian ideas, a point made by commentators.

Orthodox Marxists say it dilutes class and the economy. Perry Anderson (1976) found Gramsci ambiguous about civil society and the state. Liberals say consent in democracies is real, not false consciousness. Historians warn about "Gramsci for everyone" and about relying on fragmentary, coded prison writings written under censorship. Althusser found a historicist streak. Critics from the left ask whether a war of position never ends and never delivers.

Gramsci's notion of "subaltern classes" was borrowed by Ranajit Guha and the Subaltern Studies collective (1982), who wrote history from below. Partha Chatterjee used hegemony in Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986). Debate: the Indian National Congress gained hegemony in the freedom struggle by uniting classes under bourgeois leadership, which Gramscians call "passive revolution", a phrase Chatterjee applied to India. The BJP-RSS cultural project is often analysed as a hegemony struggle.

Key takeaways

  1. Hegemony: rule by consent through civil society, with force in reserve.
  2. War of manoeuvre versus war of position.
  3. Organic intellectuals and the historic bloc.
  4. Prison Notebooks, 1929-35, published after the war.
  5. Critics: concept is vague and dilutes class.

Debate questions

  1. Is culture or the economy the main battlefield?
  2. Does hegemony explain right-wing populism?
